questions.q: Why is true exactly-once delivery not actually achievable at the network layer?
options: A sender can never be fully certain whether a message or just its acknowledgment was lost, so retrying risks a duplicate and not retrying risks a loss
Exactly-once delivery is achievable but too expensive for most systems to bother with
Only at-most-once delivery has ever been implemented in any real system
Networks always deliver messages in the exact order they were sent
questions.explain: This is a known impossibility, not a gap in current tooling — there's no way to distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgment.

questions.q: What does 'effectively exactly-once' actually mean, as the real answer systems use?
options: At-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing, so duplicates may arrive but never change the result
A special network protocol that guarantees true exactly-once delivery
Delivering every message exactly twice to guarantee at least one success
Using at-most-once delivery exclusively to avoid any duplicates
questions.explain: The guarantee shifts from 'never sent twice' (impossible) to 'sending it twice never matters' (achievable via Lesson 11's idempotency).

questions.q: How does Databricks Autoloader's checkpointLocation demonstrate effectively-exactly-once processing?
options: It records which files have already been processed, so reprocessing an already-seen file becomes a no-op, even though delivery itself isn't guaranteed exactly-once
It guarantees the underlying file system never delivers a file more than once
It prevents any file from ever being read more than once, at the network level
Checkpoints have nothing to do with delivery guarantees
questions.explain: Delivery is at-least-once; the checkpoint is what makes the resulting processing exactly-once.

questions.q: How does Fabric's Eventstream handle a redelivered event without creating a duplicate row?
options: The destination table is MERGE-keyed on a stable event ID, so a redelivered event is absorbed without producing a duplicate
Eventstream guarantees the network layer will never redeliver any event
Eventstream discards all events after the first one received each day
Eventstream has no mechanism for handling redelivered events at all
questions.explain: This is the same MERGE-on-a-stable-key mechanism from Lesson 11, applied to a streaming destination.

questions.q: Why does idempotency (Lesson 11) matter specifically for this lesson's delivery guarantees discussion?
options: It's the mechanism that turns an achievable at-least-once delivery guarantee into an effectively-exactly-once result
Idempotency has no real connection to delivery guarantees
Idempotency only matters for batch pipelines, not streaming delivery
Idempotency replaces the need for any delivery guarantee at all
questions.explain: Lesson 11 came immediately before this lesson because idempotency is the mechanism that resolves the exactly-once impossibility, not a side note.
